title: Language core: design patterns in Java and Python
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Singleton, Factory, Builder, Strategy, Observer and Command (with undo/redo), plus Python decorators, closures and manual dependency injection, with the classic traps.
source: Gang of Four; Effective Java (Bloch); Refactoring.Guru; Python docs: functools, data model; Real Python; Baeldung

questions.prompt: Match each design pattern with its intent.

right.text: Exactly one instance with a global access point
Defer to a method or subclass to decide which concrete class to create
Construct a complex object step by step, often with many optional parts
Interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, chosen at runtime
One-to-many notification when a subject changes state
Wrap a request as an object so it can be queued, logged or undone
Convert the interface of one class into another that clients expect

questions.explanation: Adapter, the seventh item, is a structural pattern. Interviewers usually ask for one real example per pattern: java.lang.Runtime (singleton), Calendar.getInstance (factory), StringBuilder / Lombok @Builder, Comparator (strategy), event listeners (observer), Runnable / undo stacks (command).

questions.prompt: Write a thread-safe, lazily initialised Java singleton class Config using the initialization-on-demand holder idiom (or an enum).

checks.label: constructor is private (or it is an enum)
exposes it via getInstance or the enum constant

questions.explanation: The JVM initialises the Holder class lazily and exactly once, which makes it thread-safe without synchronization. enum Config { INSTANCE } is the Effective Java answer and also survives serialization and reflection. Double-checked locking needs a volatile field.

questions.prompt: Write a Java class Pizza with a required int size and an optional boolean cheese, constructed through a nested static Builder class (fluent setters and a build() method).

checks.label: has a nested static class Builder
Pizza constructor is private and takes the builder

questions.explanation: Builder avoids telescoping constructors and lets you validate in build(). Lombok @Builder or a record plus a builder generate the same. In Python, keyword arguments with defaults or a dataclass usually replace it.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: The Strategy pattern lets a program swap algorithms at runtime without long if/else chains.
questions.reason: The context object holds a reference to a strategy interface and delegates the work to it.

whys.a: Correct: delegation to an interface-typed field is the mechanism that makes swapping possible.
whys.b: R is the explanation of A, not an unrelated fact.

questions.explanation: Typical interview example: payment methods or pricing rules. In Java a lambda can be the strategy, e.g. Comparator.

options.why: The name now refers to the wrapper because the decorator did not copy metadata.
Correct: @shout rebinds hi to wrapper, and without functools.wraps its __name__ is "wrapper".
The decorator syntax is equivalent to hi = shout(hi), so it is applied.
Decoration only calls shout(hi), which returns a function without error.

questions.explanation: Always put @functools.wraps(f) on the inner function to preserve __name__, __doc__ and the signature (important for FastAPI, pytest and logging). (Verified by running it.)

questions.prompt: Write a Python decorator log_calls that prints "calling <function name>" before running the wrapped function, passes all arguments through, returns the result, and keeps the original function metadata.

checks.label: calls and returns the wrapped function

questions.explanation: A decorator is just a callable that takes a function and returns a replacement. A decorator with its own arguments needs one more level of nesting.

questions.prompt: An editor keeps an undo stack and a redo stack. The user executes commands A, B, C, D, E, then does undo, undo, redo, and finally executes a new command F. How many commands are on the undo stack at the end?
questions.explanation: After A-E: undo has 5. Two undos move E and D to redo (undo = A,B,C). Redo moves D back (undo = A,B,C,D, redo = E). Executing F pushes it and clears the redo stack: undo = A,B,C,D,F = 5 and redo = 0.

questions.prompt: Write a Java class Subject with subscribe(Consumer<String>) and publish(String) so that publishing calls every subscriber with the message.

checks.label: keeps a collection of Consumer subscribers

questions.explanation: CopyOnWriteArrayList lets a subscriber unsubscribe during notification; a plain ArrayList would throw ConcurrentModificationException then. An unsubscribe method avoids leaks.

questions.text: Instead of creating collaborators with {1} inside a class, pass them in through the constructor (constructor {2}); tests then supply a {3} or fake.
questions.explanation: Manual DI is just wiring objects in a main() or a composition root. Spring and FastAPI Depends automate the lookup but the principle (depend on abstractions, receive them from outside) is the same.

questions.prompt: Select all genuine drawbacks or pitfalls of the Singleton pattern.

options.text: It is hidden global state, which makes unit tests order-dependent and hard to mock.
options.why: A well-known criticism; prefer injecting a single shared instance.

options.text: Double-checked locking without a volatile field can publish a half-built object.
options.why: The classic broken variant before the Java 5 memory model fix.

options.text: Separate class loaders can each create their own instance.
options.why: Singleton means one per class loader, not one per JVM.

options.text: Serialization or reflection can create a second instance unless guarded.
options.why: readResolve or an enum singleton prevents this.

options.text: A Java enum singleton can be duplicated through Constructor.newInstance.
options.why: The JDK refuses to reflectively instantiate enum types.

options.text: A singleton can never be initialised lazily in a thread-safe way.
options.why: The holder idiom does exactly that.

questions.explanation: In Spring, beans are singletons per container by default, but they are managed by the container and injected, which avoids most of the global-state problems.

questions.prompt: What is the most idiomatic way to implement the Strategy pattern in Python?

options.text: Pass a function or lambda as the strategy argument
options.why: Correct: functions are first-class, so a callable replaces the whole class hierarchy.

options.text: Create an abstract Strategy class with one subclass per algorithm
options.why: Valid but ceremonial; use it when strategies hold state or need several methods.

options.text: Use a metaclass to register algorithms globally
Hard-code an if/elif chain inside the context class
options.why: That is the code smell Strategy removes.

questions.explanation: Examples: sorted(key=...), the key function of max, or a dict mapping names to callables.

questions.prompt:
A developer registers three handlers in Python:
handlers = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([h() for h in handlers])
What does it print?

options.why: That would need each lambda to capture its own value at creation time.
Correct: closures capture the variable i, not its value, and the loop leaves i == 2.
range(3) ends at 2, so i never becomes 3.
i is still alive in the enclosing scope after the comprehension via the closure cell.

questions.explanation: Fix with a default argument: lambda i=i: i, or functools.partial. The same late-binding trap hits callbacks registered in loops. (Verified by running it.)

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: An Observer implementation that holds strong references to its listeners can cause a memory leak.
questions.reason: Listeners are garbage collected automatically as soon as they leave their local scope, even while they are still registered.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (the lapsed listener problem); R is false, because a registered listener is still reachable from the subject.

questions.explanation: Always provide unsubscribe, or hold listeners through WeakReference (Java) or weakref.WeakSet (Python).

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: Python decorators can only be applied to functions, never to classes.
questions.reason: A decorator is any callable that receives an object and returns a replacement or the same object.

whys.a: A is false, so it cannot be right.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: class decorators exist (for example @dataclass), so A is false; R correctly defines a decorator.

questions.explanation: @dataclass, @functools.total_ordering and many registries are class decorators.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A Java enum with one constant is a safe way to implement a Singleton.

whys.a: Both true, but implementing interfaces is not why it is safe; safety comes from JVM-guaranteed one-time instantiation and protection against reflection and serialization.
whys.b: Correct: both statements are true, yet R does not explain A.
whys.d: A is true; Effective Java recommends this approach.

questions.explanation: Limitation: the enum cannot extend another class, and it is eagerly loaded when the enum class initialises.
